docs.title: Overview
docs.description: Framework-agnostic grid logic: columns, sizing, ordering, selection, sorting, filtering, row grouping, pagination and more.
docs.body:
@gridkitjs/core is plain TypeScript — so it's testable without a DOM and reusable from other framework adapters. It holds everything the grid decides: column inference, sizing, ordering, selection, sorting, the filtering engine, row grouping, aggregates, pagination, virtualization math, and keyboard navigation. A renderer such as @gridkitjs/react draws the result.

## The view pipeline

[resolveGridView](/docs/core/view) composes the stages into the one view a [renderer](/docs/react#terms) draws: rows are filtered → sorted → grouped → aggregated → paginated, and columns are ordered → hidden → sized. A page never splits a top-level group, and aggregates are computed before pagination, so a subtotal never depends on which page is showing. createGridViewResolver is its memoised form, which recomputes only the stages a change touches.

## Grid options

`GridOptions<Row>` is every setting of a grid that names no renderer's types: `dataSource` and `getRowId`, what the user may do (`sortableColumns`, `selectable`, `paginated`…), the state it starts in (`defaultColumnSort`, `defaultPagination`…), the callbacks that report changes (`onColumnSortChange`…), the row hooks (`onRowClick`, `onRowDoubleClick`, and `getRowProps` for a row's class and `data-*` attributes), `locale`, `messages`, `contextMenu` and `onContextMenuOpenChange` (see [context menus](/docs/core/commands#context-menus)), `commands` and `onCommand` (see [app commands](/docs/core/commands#on-a-grid)), and `toolbar` (see [toolbar](/docs/core/toolbar#the-option)). A renderer's own props are these plus what only it can express — @gridkitjs/react's `DataGridProps` adds `columns`, the pager and infinite-scroll templates, `renderToolbarItem`, the selection callbacks and `ref` — so a setting means the same thing, under the same name, in every renderer.

### Messages

`GridMessages` is every string a grid shows or announces of its own — the pager, the group-by bar, the loading row, boolean and blank values, the built-in commands' labels, the menus' names, the toolbar's name, search box and "More" button, the column chooser's name, search box and "Show all", and the live-region announcements. `defaultMessages` holds the English a grid speaks unless told otherwise, its counts grouped in the runtime's locale; `createDefaultMessages(locale)` is the same English counting in `locale`'s digits — "1,204 of 10,000 rows" under `"en"`, "1.204 of 10.000 rows" under `"de-DE"`. `resolveMessages(messages, locale)` lays a partial `messages` option over the defaults for `locale`, returning the defaults themselves — the same object for the same locale — when given none. A message naming something is a function — `pageStatus: (page, pageCount) => string` — so a translation puts the name where its grammar wants it. See [localization](/docs/react/localization) for every key.

## The controller

[createGridController](/docs/core/controller) holds a grid's state, derives its view and carries every action a user can take, with each slice of state controlled or uncontrolled on its own. A renderer creates one per grid, feeds it its options and draws the view, so the renderer decides nothing the user can see.

## Commands and menus

A [command](/docs/core/commands) is the one implementation behind a menu item, a toolbar button and the API — "Sort ascending", "Hide column", "Clear filters". It decides whether it shows and whether it can run from a snapshot of the grid, and acts through the controller's actions. `builtInCommands` is the grid's own set; `resolveCommands` lays an app's commands over it, replacing a built-in by id. A menu is a list of command ids, separators, inline items and submenus, which `resolveMenu` turns into what a renderer draws.

## Filters and filter editors

A filter is plain data — operator entries such as `{ columnId: "amount", operator: "between", value: [10, 100] }` save and restore with the rest of the state. The [filter-editor model](/docs/core/filtering) is what a column's filter UI is drawn over: the shape of the column's filter, its values with counts cascaded over the other filters, and a draft reducer for a checklist or condition editor.

## Install

<PackageInstall pkg="@gridkitjs/core" />

`@gridkitjs/react` already depends on it; install it yourself only to import from it directly. See [choosing packages](/docs/react/choosing-packages) for which package an app needs.

See [column definitions](/docs/core/column-definitions) for column inference, [resizing](/docs/core/resizing) and [ordering](/docs/core/ordering) for the logic underneath resizableColumns and reorderableColumns, or [selection](/docs/core/selection) for the primitives underneath selectable.

## See also

- [React quick start](/docs/react/overview) for the React renderer and its glossary.
- [Choosing packages](/docs/react/choosing-packages) for which package to install.
- [Controller](/docs/core/controller) for the entry point to everything else.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.description: The pagination logic underneath paginated and the numbered pager.
docs.body:
`paginateRows` slices the grid's rows into pages, and `paginationWindow` works out which page numbers a numbered pager shows. The [view pipeline](/docs/core/view) pages for you under `paginated`; reach for these directly in a custom adapter or a pager of your own.

A `PaginationState` is `{ pageIndex, pageSize }`, with `pageIndex` 0-based.

## Functions

| Function                                             | Type                               | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `paginateRows(rows, pagination)`                     | `PaginatedRows<Row>`               | The page `pagination` names, from rows already filtered, sorted, grouped and aggregated. A `pageIndex` out of range is clamped, and a `pageSize` below `1` is taken as `1`.                                                    |
| `paginationWindow(currentPage, pageCount, options?)` | `readonly PaginationWindowEntry[]` | The 1-based page numbers a numbered pager shows for `currentPage` of `pageCount`, always the same number of entries once there are more pages than fit. `options` is `{ boundaryCount?, siblingCount? }`, both `1` by default. |

A page counts **units**, not rows: a top-level group with everything under it is one unit, as is a bare data row outside any group, so a group never splits across pages and a page of 25 holds 25 top-level groups when the grid is grouped. A group's summary row stays with its group.

`PaginatedRows<Row>` is what `paginateRows` returns:

| Field       | Type                         | Description                                                                                                                          |
| ----------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `rows`      | `readonly DisplayRow<Row>[]` | The page's rows, with `rowIndex` renumbered from `0` at the top of the page. `datasetIndex` keeps each row's place in the whole set. |
| `pageCount` | `number`                     | How many pages the rows make at this size — `0` for no rows.                                                                         |
| `pageIndex` | `number`                     | The page returned: `pagination.pageIndex`, clamped. Read this back rather than trusting the one passed in.                           |

```ts
import { paginateRows, paginationWindow } from "@gridkitjs/core";

const page = paginateRows(displayRows, { pageIndex: 6, pageSize: 25 });
page.pageIndex; // 6, or the last page if there are fewer than 7

paginationWindow(page.pageIndex + 1, page.pageCount);
// [1, "ellipsis", 6, 7, 8, "ellipsis", 20] for page 7 of 20
```

`paginationWindow` always keeps the first and last `boundaryCount` pages and a run of `2 * siblingCount + 1` pages around the current one, slid inwards near either end rather than cut short. Between each boundary and that run sits one slot: the page it skips when it skips only one, an `"ellipsis"` otherwise.

So the window has a constant length. Once `pageCount` is more than `2 * boundaryCount + 2 * siblingCount + 3` (7 with the defaults), every page's window has exactly that many entries, and a pager that gives each entry the same width keeps its next and last buttons in place as the user pages through. Up to that many pages, every page shows.

```ts
paginationWindow(1, 20); // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, "ellipsis", 20]
paginationWindow(10, 20); // [1, "ellipsis", 9, 10, 11, "ellipsis", 20]
paginationWindow(20, 20); // [1, "ellipsis", 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]
```

## In the React grid

`paginated` and `pager` turn pagination on — see [pagination](/docs/react/pagination).

## See also

- [Pagination](/docs/react/pagination) for the React grid.
- [The view pipeline](/docs/core/view) for where pagination runs.
- [Controller](/docs/core/controller) for `pagination` as controller state.

docs.title: Resizing
docs.description: The sizing logic underneath resizableColumns.
docs.body:
`resolveColumnWidths` and `fitColumnsToWidth` are the functions DataGrid calls internally when `resizableColumns` is enabled — the first resolves each column's width from its definition, the sizing state, and the grid's defaults, the second redistributes width across columns under `resizeMode`="fit". Reach for them directly if you're building a custom grid adapter.

## Functions

| Function                                                             | Type                             | Description                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `resolveColumnWidths(columns, sizing, options)`                      | `readonly ResolvedColumn<Row>[]` | Resolves each column's rendered width from its definition, the sizing state, and the grid's defaults.                               |
| `fitColumnsToWidth(columns, width, sizeDefaults)`                    | `readonly ResolvedColumn<Row>[]` | Redistributes width across columns under resizeMode="fit".                                                                          |
| `clampColumnWidth(width, constraints)`                               | `number`                         | Holds a width within a column's min/max bounds.                                                                                     |
| `resolveColumnConstraints(column, sizeDefaults)`                     | `ColumnConstraints`              | The min/max a column may be resized between.                                                                                        |
| `beginColumnResize(column, startWidth, startPosition, sizeDefaults)` | `ColumnResizeSession`            | Opens a resize: captures the column's constraints and starting point so applying a pointer position is arithmetic on numbers alone. |
| `applyColumnResize(session, position)`                               | `number`                         | The width the dragged column takes with the pointer at position.                                                                    |
| `sizeColumnToContent(measuredWidth, constraints)`                    | `number`                         | The width a double-click autofit resolves to, clamped to the column's bounds.                                                       |
| `totalColumnWidth(resolved)`                                         | `number`                         | The sum of every resolved column's width.                                                                                           |
| `revertColumnSize(current, base, columnId)`                          | `ColumnSizingState`              | The sizing state with columnId reverted to its width in base — or omitted entirely if base had none — for Escape to restore.        |

| Constant               | Value                                              | Description                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DEFAULT_COLUMN_SIZES` | `{ width: 150, minWidth: 40, maxWidth: Infinity }` | The `ColumnSizeDefaults` a column falls back to when neither it nor `columnSizeDefaults` sizes it.          |
| `KEYBOARD_STEP`        | `10`                                               | Pixels one <Kbd>Alt</Kbd>+<Kbd>ArrowLeft</Kbd> or <Kbd>Alt</Kbd>+<Kbd>ArrowRight</Kbd> moves a column edge. |

## The same logic, in the React grid

<ColumnResizingExample />

## See also

- [Column resizing](/docs/react/column-resizing) for the React grid.
- [Column definitions](/docs/core/column-definitions) for the `width`, `minWidth` and `maxWidth` fields.
- [Ordering](/docs/core/ordering) for the column order.

docs.title: Selection
docs.description: The selection primitives underneath selectable.
docs.body:
These transforms are what a click, a <Kbd>Ctrl</Kbd>+click, and a <Kbd>Shift</Kbd>+click each reduce to — every one takes the selection it received and returns the selection after, never touching a DOM node or a row of data. The [controller](/docs/core/controller)'s selection actions are built on them, so every renderer selects the same way.

## Functions

| Function                                                                  | Type                             | Description                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `toggleSelection(selection, id, mode)`                                    | `SelectionState`                 | Adds id if absent, removes it if present — a <Kbd>Ctrl</Kbd>+click, or <Kbd>Space</Kbd> on the focused member.                       |
| `selectOnly(selection, id, mode)`                                         | `SelectionState`                 | The selection reduced to id alone — a plain click. Never deselects, so clicking the one selected row leaves it selected.             |
| `selectRange(selection, orderedIds, anchorId, focusId, mode)`             | `SelectionState`                 | Every id from anchorId to focusId inclusive, spanning orderedIds — a <Kbd>Shift</Kbd>+click. Degrades to selectOnly under "single".  |
| `selectAll(selection, orderedIds, mode)`                                  | `SelectionState`                 | Every id in orderedIds, or selection untouched under any mode but "multiple".                                                        |
| `clearSelection(selection)`                                               | `SelectionState`                 | Empties the selection.                                                                                                               |
| `diffSelection(previous, next)`                                           | `SelectionDiff`                  | What one transition added and removed — the one place a select and a deselect fired for the same interaction cannot disagree.        |
| `selectCell(selection, cell, mode)`                                       | `CellSelectionState`             | Moves the cell selection to cell — a plain click. Idempotent: clicking the selected cell again leaves it selected.                   |
| `toggleCellSelection(selection, cell, mode)`                              | `CellSelectionState`             | Moves to cell, or clears when it is already there — a <Kbd>Ctrl</Kbd>+click.                                                         |
| `isSameCell(a, b)`                                                        | `boolean`                        | Whether two cell selections address the same row and column.                                                                         |
| `intentOf(event, options?)`                                               | `SelectIntent`                   | Reads a click or key press's modifiers into "replace", "toggle", or "range". `{ toggleOnClick: true }` makes a plain press a toggle. |
| `applySelectionIntent(selection, orderedIds, anchorId, id, intent, mode)` | `SelectionState`                 | Dispatches an intent to toggleSelection, selectRange, or selectOnly.                                                                 |
| `resolveRows(rowsById, ids)`                                              | `readonly ResolvedRow<Row>[]`    | Resolves selected ids back to the rows behind them, dropping any id whose row no longer exists.                                      |
| `resolveColumns(columns, ids)`                                            | `readonly SelectedColumn<Row>[]` | Resolves selected ids back to their column and position, dropping any id whose column no longer exists.                              |
| `resolveCell(rowsById, columns, cell)`                                    | `SelectedCell<Row> \| null`      | Resolves a cell selection down to its row, column, and value — null if either no longer exists.                                      |

A grid's `selectable` option is a `SelectableConfig` — `{ rows?, columns?, cells?, toggleOnClick? }` — giving each `mode` above: `rows` and `columns` take a `SelectionMode`, `false`, `"single"` or `"multiple"`, and `cells` a `CellSelectionMode`, `false` or `"single"`. All are off by default. `toggleOnClick` makes a plain click on a row toggle it, as `intentOf`'s `{ toggleOnClick: true }` does.

## The same logic, in the React grid

<CombinedSelectionExample />

## See also

- [Row selection](/docs/react/row-selection), [column selection](/docs/react/column-selection) and [cell selection](/docs/react/cell-selection) for the React grid.
- [Controller](/docs/core/controller) for the selection state.
- [Focus and virtualization](/docs/core/navigation) for focus, which selection follows.

docs.title: Sorting
docs.description: The comparator and sort transforms underneath sortableColumns.
docs.body:
`sortRows` and `toggleColumnSort` are the functions a grid sorts with — the first orders rows by a `ColumnSortState`, the second works out the state a header click leads to. The [view pipeline](/docs/core/view) and the [controller](/docs/core/controller) call them for you; reach for them directly to sort rows outside a grid, or in a custom adapter.

A `ColumnSortState` is `readonly ColumnSortEntry[]`, each entry `{ columnId, direction }` with `direction` a `SortDirection` — `"asc"` or `"desc"` — in priority order: the first entry sorts, the second breaks its ties, and so on.

## Functions

| Function                                    | Type                          | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sortRows(rows, sort, columns)`             | `readonly ResolvedRow<Row>[]` | `rows` ordered by `sort`, each entry read against `columns` for its field and type, with `rowIndex` renumbered. Stable; a blank value sorts last in either direction. Returns `rows` itself for an empty sort, or one naming only absent columns. |
| `compareValues(a, b, type?)`                | `number`                      | Compares two cell values as `type` says — numerically for the numeric types, chronologically for the date and time types, `false` before `true`, and as text otherwise or with no type. `null` and `undefined` sort after every value.            |
| `toggleColumnSort(sort, columnId, options)` | `ColumnSortState`             | `columnId` cycled to its next direction, none → ascending → descending → none. `{ stack: false }`, a plain click, sorts by that column alone; `{ stack: true }`, a <Kbd>Shift</Kbd>+click, cycles it in place and leaves the rest.                |
| `sortDirectionFor(sort, columnId)`          | `SortDirection \| null`       | This column's direction in `sort`, or `null` when it does not sort.                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `sortPriorityFor(sort, columnId)`           | `number \| null`              | This column's 1-based place in `sort`, or `null` when it does not sort — what a header's priority badge shows.                                                                                                                                    |

`compareValues` is also what grouping orders its group values with, what `min` and `max` [aggregates](/docs/core/aggregation) compare by, and how a filter checklist orders its values.

```ts
import { sortRows, toggleColumnSort } from "@gridkitjs/core";

let sort = toggleColumnSort([], "Region", { stack: false }); // Region ascending
sort = toggleColumnSort(sort, "Amount", { stack: true }); // then Amount ascending

const sorted = sortRows(rows, sort, dataColumns);
```

`rows` are `ResolvedRow`s and `columns` the width-free `DataColumn`s [`resolveDataColumns`](/docs/core/ordering) returns — the shapes the view pipeline passes between its stages.

## In the React grid

`sortableColumns` turns the header's sort toggle on — see [column sorting](/docs/react/column-sorting).

## See also

- [Column sorting](/docs/react/column-sorting) for the React grid.
- [The view pipeline](/docs/core/view) for where sorting runs.
- [Server-side data](/docs/react/server-side-data) for sorting that happens on a server.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.description: ToolbarEntry and resolveToolbar: a toolbar written in the menu vocabulary, and the arithmetic that moves what does not fit into a More menu.
docs.body:
A toolbar is written in the same vocabulary as a [menu](/docs/core/commands#menus): a command id is a button, an inline item a button of its own, a submenu a dropdown button and `"separator"` a separator — plus three entries only a toolbar has. Core resolves the entries against the grid's state, so a button is disabled, pressed or gone exactly when its command says, and works out how many fit; a renderer draws the result and attaches @gridkitjs/dom's [toolbar behaviours](/docs/dom/menus-and-toolbar#toolbar).

```ts
import type { ToolbarEntry } from "@gridkitjs/core";

const toolbar: readonly ToolbarEntry<Order>[] = [
  "search",
  "separator",
  "sort.clearAll",
  "filter.clearAll",
  {
    type: "submenu",
    id: "groups",
    label: "Groups",
    items: ["group.expandAll", "group.collapseAll", "group.clearAll"],
  },
  "spacer",
  { type: "custom", id: "orders.status" },
];
```

## Entries

A `ToolbarEntry<Row>` is any `MenuEntry<Row>` or one of the toolbar's own:

| Entry                                      | Drawn as                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"filter.clearAll"`                        | A command's button. A checkable command is a toggle button, pressed while checked.                                                  |
| `{ type: "item", id, label, onSelect, … }` | A button of its own, with an inline item's fields; a toggle when it has `checked`.                                                  |
| `{ type: "submenu", id, label, items }`    | A dropdown button opening a menu of `items`.                                                                                        |
| `"separator"`                              | A separator.                                                                                                                        |
| `"search"`                                 | The search box, over the filter's global text entry — see [a search box](/docs/core/filtering#a-search-box).                        |
| `"spacer"`                                 | The free space, pushing what follows it to the far end. Two spacers share it.                                                       |
| `"export"`                                 | An "Export" dropdown of the [export commands](/docs/core/commands#built-in-commands) that show — see [below](#the-export-dropdown). |
| `{ type: "custom", id }`                   | A `ToolbarCustomEntry`: a place the renderer fills with content of yours — in @gridkitjs/react, what `renderToolbarItem` draws.     |

Like `"separator"`, the strings `"search"`, `"spacer"` and `"export"` are the toolbar's own: a toolbar reads them as its entries, never as command ids.

The built-ins meant for a toolbar are `sort.clearAll`, `group.clearAll`, `group.expandAll`, `group.collapseAll`, `column.autoFitAll`, `column.choose`, `filter.clearAll` and the exports — see [built-in commands](/docs/core/commands#built-in-commands). The rest act on a column, a row or a group, which a toolbar has none of, so they never show in one.

### The export dropdown

`"export"` stands for a dropdown, keyed and identified `"export"` and labelled `messages.exportMenu`, listing `export.csv`, `export.json`, `export.xlsx` and `export.pdf`, then a separator and `exportSelection.csv`, `exportSelection.json` and `exportSelection.xlsx`. Each hides where it cannot act — xlsx and PDF until a writer for them is registered, the selection exports while no row is selected — so the dropdown lists what the grid can export now: CSV and JSON on a grid with no writers of its own. With nothing to list it is left out, like any dropdown.

```ts
toolbar={{ items: ["search", "spacer", "export", "column.choose"] }}
```

For a different list — a single CSV button, or exports beside other actions — write the entries yourself: `"export.csv"` alone, or a `submenu` of the ids you want.

## The option

A grid's `toolbar` option — `boolean | GridToolbarOptions<Row>` — says whether it has a toolbar and what it lists. `true` lists `defaultToolbar`; an object lists its `items` (the defaults when it leaves them out) and may name the toolbar for a screen reader with `label`, which is otherwise `messages.toolbarLabel`.

| Field   | Type                           | Description                                      |
| ------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `items` | `readonly ToolbarEntry<Row>[]` | The entries, in order. Defaults to the defaults. |
| `label` | `string`                       | The toolbar's accessible name.                   |

`defaultToolbar` is the search box, a spacer, `filter.clearAll` and `column.choose`: search on the left, "Clear filters" and "Choose columns" at the far end. Exporting is not among the defaults; list `"export"` to add it. `toolbarEntries(toolbar)` reads the option — no entries while it is off, else the defaults or its `items` — for `resolveToolbar` to resolve.

## Resolving

`resolveToolbar(entries, { commands, contextFor })` — a `ToolbarResolveOptions` — resolves a toolbar against the grid and returns the `ResolvedToolbarItem[]` to draw, by `resolveMenu`'s rules: hidden commands and items are left out, and so is an id naming no command, reported once per command map with a `console.error`; labels become strings and flags booleans; `"export"` becomes the [export dropdown](#the-export-dropdown); a dropdown whose items all hide is left out; and separators never lead, trail, double up — or sit beside a spacer, which already parts what is on either side of it.

Each item resolves and runs in a context of its own, from `contextFor(target)`: its target is a `GridToolbarTarget`, `{ area: "toolbar", itemId }`, naming the item — or, for an item in a dropdown, the dropdown — so a command opening a [panel](/docs/core/commands#panels), as `column.choose` does, can anchor it there.

```ts
import {
  createCommandContext,
  resolveCommands,
  resolveToolbar,
  toolbarEntries,
} from "@gridkitjs/core";

const commands = resolveCommands(options.commands);

function draw() {
  const items = resolveToolbar(toolbarEntries(options.toolbar), {
    commands,
    contextFor: (target) =>
      createCommandContext({ controller, target, messages, host }),
  });
  render(items);
}
controller.subscribe(draw); // resolve again on every change
```

| Resolved item           | Fields                                                                                                                            |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ResolvedToolbarButton` | `type: "button"`, `id`, `key`, `label`, `icon`, `shortcut`, `disabled`, `pressed` (`boolean \| undefined`, for a toggle), `run()` |
| `ResolvedToolbarMenu`   | `type: "menu"`, `id`, `key`, `label`, `icon`, `items` — resolved menu entries, never empty                                        |
| `ResolvedToolbarSearch` | `type: "search"`, `key`                                                                                                           |
| `ResolvedToolbarSpacer` | `type: "spacer"`, `key`                                                                                                           |
| `ResolvedMenuSeparator` | `type: "separator"`, `key`                                                                                                        |
| `ResolvedToolbarCustom` | `type: "custom"`, `id`, `key`                                                                                                     |

Every item has a `key`, unique among the toolbar's: an item's id, `"search"`, or `separator-<index>` and `spacer-<index>` from the entry's place in the list. A renderer writes it into the element's `data-gridkit-toolbar-item`, which @gridkitjs/dom's behaviours find entries by. `run()` runs a button against its context and says whether it ran, as a menu item's does.

## Overflow

When the toolbar is narrower than its items, the ones that do not fit go into a "More" menu button at its end. The search box and custom entries stay however narrow it gets — they have no menu item to become; `isPinnedToolbarItem(item)` says which entries those are.

`fitToolbarItems({ widths, available, moreWidth, pinned })` — a `ToolbarFitInput` — decides how many fit, given each entry's width and whether it is pinned, the width they share and the More button's. It returns a count: the first `count` entries stay, with every pinned entry after them, and the rest overflow.

- Pinned entries take their room first, wherever they are.
- Room for More is kept only when something overflows. When everything fits, the count is every entry.
- Entries are taken in order, and the first that does not fit ends the count — the toolbar keeps its order rather than filling the gap with a later, narrower entry. A spacer's width is only the space left over, so it counts as `0` and fits wherever the entries before it did.

`splitToolbarItems(items, count)` splits a resolved toolbar there into a `ToolbarSplit`: `shown`, what stays, and `overflow`, the More menu's entries — each button an item, checked where it was pressed, each dropdown a submenu, spacers left out — with separators collapsed on both sides. The More menu's items run exactly as the buttons would have.

```ts
import {
  fitToolbarItems,
  isPinnedToolbarItem,
  splitToolbarItems,
} from "@gridkitjs/core";

const count = fitToolbarItems({
  widths: items.map((item) => (item.type === "spacer" ? 0 : widthOf(item.key))),
  available: toolbarWidth,
  moreWidth,
  pinned: items.map(isPinnedToolbarItem),
});
const { shown, overflow } = splitToolbarItems(items, count);
```

@gridkitjs/dom's [`observeToolbarOverflow`](/docs/dom/menus-and-toolbar#toolbar) does the measuring and calls `fitToolbarItems` for you.

| Function                           | Type                             | Description                                                                           |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `toolbarEntries(toolbar)`          | `readonly ToolbarEntry<Row>[]`   | The entries the `toolbar` option lists: none while off, else the defaults or `items`. |
| `resolveToolbar(entries, options)` | `readonly ResolvedToolbarItem[]` | The entries resolved against the grid, ready to draw.                                 |
| `fitToolbarItems(input)`           | `number`                         | How many entries fit, from the start.                                                 |
| `isPinnedToolbarItem(item)`        | `boolean`                        | Whether an entry stays however narrow the toolbar gets: search and custom entries.    |
| `splitToolbarItems(items, count)`  | `ToolbarSplit`                   | What stays, and the More menu's entries.                                              |

## See also

- [Toolbar](/docs/react/toolbar) for the React component.
- [Commands and menus](/docs/core/commands) for the commands the items run.
- [@gridkitjs/dom](/docs/dom) for the toolbar behaviour.

docs.title: The view pipeline
docs.description: resolveGridView: rows, columns, state and options in; everything the grid shows out.
docs.body:
`resolveGridView` is the one function that answers "what is the user looking at". It takes the rows, the column definitions, the grid's state and its options, and runs every stage DataGrid renders from: rows are filtered → sorted → grouped → aggregated → paginated, and columns are ordered → hidden → sized. Call it from a custom adapter, an export or a toolbar instead of composing the stages yourself, so nothing can disagree with what the grid shows.

```ts
import { resolveGridView } from "@gridkitjs/core";

const view = resolveGridView({
  rows,
  getRowId: (row) => String(row.Id),
  columns,
  state: {
    columnSizing: {},
    columnOrder: [],
    columnVisibility: {},
    columnSort: [{ columnId: "Amount", direction: "desc" }],
    filter: [],
    groupBy: [{ columnId: "Region" }],
    groupExpansion: [],
    pagination: { pageIndex: 0, pageSize: 25 },
  },
  options: { paginated: true, aggregates: [{ columnId: "Amount", fn: "sum" }] },
});

view.pageRows; // the current page: group headers and data rows, in render order
view.grandTotal.get("Amount"); // the sum over every filtered row, on every page
```

## Functions

| Function                                        | Type                                 | Description                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `resolveGridView(input)`                        | `GridView<Row, Node>`                | Derives the whole view in one call, with no memory of earlier calls.                                                                                                         |
| `createGridViewResolver()`                      | `(input: GridViewInput) => GridView` | A memoised `resolveGridView`. Each stage keeps its last inputs and returns its last output when none changed, so a call recomputes only what a change touches.               |
| `resolveShownRows(rows, filter, sort, columns)` | `readonly ResolvedRow<Row>[]`        | The data stages before grouping on their own: `rows` filtered with `filterRows`, then sorted with `sortRows`. Filtering first only saves work; the order comes out the same. |

## `GridView`

| Field             | Type                             | Description                                                                                                                         |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dataColumns`     | `readonly DataColumn<Row>[]`     | Every column, hidden ones included, ordered, as `{ id, column }` — no width. What filtering, sorting, grouping and aggregates read. |
| `columns`         | `readonly ResolvedColumn<Row>[]` | The columns as rendered: visible, ordered and sized.                                                                                |
| `rows`            | `readonly ResolvedRow<Row>[]`    | The rows, filtered then sorted.                                                                                                     |
| `displayRows`     | `readonly DisplayRow<Row>[]`     | `rows` grouped, each group header carrying its aggregates — every page.                                                             |
| `pageRows`        | `readonly DisplayRow<Row>[]`     | The current page of `displayRows`. All of it when not paginated. A page never splits a top-level group.                             |
| `displayDataRows` | `readonly ResolvedRow<Row>[]`    | `pageRows` without group headers or summary rows — the data rows on screen, in display order.                                       |
| `pageCount`       | `number`                         | `1` when not paginated.                                                                                                             |
| `pageIndex`       | `number`                         | The page shown, clamped into range. `0` when not paginated.                                                                         |
| `grandTotal`      | `AggregateResults`               | Every aggregate over all of `rows`, ignoring grouping and pagination.                                                               |

## Input

`state` is a `GridViewState<Row>`: `columnSizing`, `columnOrder`, `columnVisibility`, `columnSort`, `filter`, `groupBy`, `groupExpansion` and `pagination`, each the same type as the matching `default*` prop on DataGrid — every slice of `GridState` but the three selections, which change what is highlighted and never what is shown, so a whole `GridState` serves too. `options` is a `GridViewOptions<Row>`; every field is optional and defaults the way DataGrid's prop of the same name does:

| Option                                                              | Default    | Description                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `paginated`                                                         | `false`    | Whether `pageRows` is one page rather than every row.                                        |
| `aggregates`                                                        | `[]`       | The aggregates to compute, per group and in `grandTotal`.                                    |
| `groupAggregateDisplay`                                             | `"inline"` | `"row"` adds a summary row after each group.                                                 |
| `columnSizeDefaults`                                                | —          | Width and bounds for a column that sets none.                                                |
| `resizableColumns`, `reorderableColumns`, `groupByDraggableColumns` | `false`    | Grid-level defaults a column's own setting overrides.                                        |
| `resizeMode`                                                        | `"fit"`    | `"fit"` stretches or squeezes columns to fill `viewportWidth`; `"fixed"` keeps their widths. |
| `viewportWidth`                                                     | `null`     | The width to fit. Leave it out where there is no viewport, such as an export.                |

A column hidden by its definition's `hidden` or by `columnVisibility` leaves `columns` but stays in `dataColumns`, so a sort, filter or grouping on it still applies, and it keeps its slot in the column order for when it is shown again. `isColumnVisible(column, visibility)` answers for one column, `applyColumnVisibility(dataColumns, visibility)` drops the hidden ones, and `setColumnVisibility(dataColumns, visibility, columnIds, visible)` returns the next state, or the same one when nothing changes.

`columns` is used as given: inferring columns from the rows when a grid is given none is the [controller](/docs/core/controller)'s job, done before it resolves the view.

## Memoisation

Hold one `createGridViewResolver()` per grid and call it with the current input whenever the view is needed. Stages compare their inputs by identity, so pass state slices as the same objects until they change. The data stages read `dataColumns`, which carry no width, so a resize or a viewport change re-sizes `columns` and leaves `rows`, `displayRows`, `pageRows`, `displayDataRows` and `grandTotal` exactly as they were — the same references. The returned view object itself is reused when nothing in it changed.

```ts
const resolve = createGridViewResolver<Row>();

const before = resolve(input);
const after = resolve({
  ...input,
  state: { ...input.state, columnSizing: { Amount: 180 } },
});

after.rows === before.rows; // true — filtering and sorting did not run again
after.columns === before.columns; // false — the widths changed
```

## See also

- [Controller](/docs/core/controller) for the state the pipeline reads.
- [Filtering](/docs/core/filtering), [sorting](/docs/core/sorting), [row grouping](/docs/core/grouping) and [pagination](/docs/core/paging) for the stages in order.
- [React quick start](/docs/react/overview) for the glossary entry on the view pipeline.

docs.title: Observers and virtualizer
docs.description: observeElementWidth, createRowVirtualizer and attachInfiniteScroll: the observers behind fit-to-width, row virtualization and infinite scroll.
docs.body:
Three behaviours that watch the page's layout and report what it means for the grid: `observeElementWidth` reports the width `resizeMode: "fit"` fills, `createRowVirtualizer` the window of rows near the scroll position, and `attachInfiniteScroll` the moment the next load should start. Each owns its observers and listeners, and stops with the function or object it returns.

## Element width

`observeElementWidth(element, onWidth)` reports `element.clientWidth` straight away and again whenever it changes, and returns the function that stops it — the width `resizeMode: "fit"` fills, passed to the controller as `viewportWidth`. The first report is synchronous, so columns laid out before paint never show at the wrong width for a frame.

```ts
import { observeElementWidth } from "@gridkitjs/dom";

const disconnect = observeElementWidth(viewportElement, (width) => {
  controller.setOptions({ ...options, viewportWidth: width });
});
```

## Row virtualizer

`createRowVirtualizer(scrollElement, { estimatedRowHeight, overscan, onRange })` windows a long list of rows inside a scrolling element down to those near its scroll position. It measures each rendered row's real height — rows need not be uniform — and reports the window to render through `onRange({ startIndex, endIndex, offsetBefore, offsetAfter })`, with `offsetBefore`/`offsetAfter` the heights of the spacers that stand in for the rows outside it. It reports only when the window moves.

| Member                          | Description                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `setRowCount(count)`            | How many rows there are. Heights measured for rows that remain are kept.                                                   |
| `resetHeights()`                | Forgets every measured height — after a sort or filter, when the rows at each index are different rows.                    |
| `measureRow(index)`             | A ref callback for row `index`'s element, measuring it while mounted. The same function for the same index every time.     |
| `scrollToIndex(index, options)` | Scrolls a mounted row into view; jumps to an unmounted one's estimated offset, then scrolls to it properly once it mounts. |
| `destroy()`                     | Stops listening and measuring.                                                                                             |

```ts
import { createRowVirtualizer } from "@gridkitjs/dom";

const virtualizer = createRowVirtualizer(bodyElement, {
  estimatedRowHeight: 40,
  overscan: 4,
  onRange: (range) => drawRows(range), // rows startIndex..endIndex, between two spacers
});
virtualizer.setRowCount(rows.length);

// while drawing row `index`:
virtualizer.measureRow(index)(rowElement);
```

The arithmetic is @gridkitjs/core's `visibleRange`; this owns the measured heights, the scroll and resize listeners, and one `ResizeObserver` for every mounted row.

## Infinite scroll

`attachInfiniteScroll(root, options)` calls `onLoadMore` as a sentinel element — the last row of the body — comes within `rootMargin` of the scrolling `root`, at most once until `isLoadingMore` has gone from `true` back to `false`. It returns `update(options)`, which a renderer calls after every render with the current options and sentinel (the sentinel comes and goes with `hasMore`), and `detach()`.

```ts
import { attachInfiniteScroll } from "@gridkitjs/dom";

const scroll = attachInfiniteScroll(bodyElement, {
  sentinel: lastRow,
  hasMore: true,
  onLoadMore: () => fetchNextPage(),
});

// after each render
scroll.update({ sentinel: lastRow, hasMore, isLoadingMore, onLoadMore });
scroll.detach();
```

`options` is an `InfiniteScrollOptions`:

| Option          | Type              | Description                                                                                                                                        |
| --------------- | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sentinel`      | `Element \| null` | The element whose approach triggers a load — the body's always-last row — or `null` while none is rendered.                                        |
| `hasMore`       | `boolean`         | Whether a further load could still return more rows. `false` stops watching altogether.                                                            |
| `onLoadMore`    | `() => void`      | Called at most once per approach, and not again until `isLoadingMore` has gone from `true` back to `false`.                                        |
| `isLoadingMore` | `boolean`         | Whether a load `onLoadMore` started is still in flight. Defaults to `false`.                                                                       |
| `rootMargin`    | `string`          | How far ahead of the sentinel scrolling into view a load starts, as CSS margins — an `IntersectionObserver`'s `rootMargin`. Defaults to `"200px"`. |

`update` is cheap when nothing changed; a new sentinel or `rootMargin` restarts the observer, and `isLoadingMore` going back to `false` checks again at once.

When a load finishes but the rows it appended leave the sentinel still in range, the next load starts straight away — nothing would scroll it out and back in to trigger one. With `hasMore` false or no sentinel, nothing is observed.

## Types

| Type                    | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `RowVirtualizerOptions` | `{ estimatedRowHeight, overscan, onRange }` for `createRowVirtualizer`. `onRange` receives the `VisibleRange` from `@gridkitjs/core`, `{ startIndex, endIndex, offsetBefore, offsetAfter }`, with `endIndex` inclusive. |
| `RowVirtualizer`        | `{ setRowCount, resetHeights, measureRow, scrollToIndex, destroy }`, what `createRowVirtualizer` returns; tabled under [row virtualizer](#row-virtualizer).                                                             |
| `InfiniteScrollOptions` | `{ sentinel, hasMore, onLoadMore?, isLoadingMore?, rootMargin? }`, tabled under [infinite scroll](#infinite-scroll).                                                                                                    |
| `InfiniteScroll`        | `{ update, detach }`, what `attachInfiniteScroll` returns.                                                                                                                                                              |

## See also

- [Gestures and focus](/docs/dom/gestures-and-focus) for the focus controller that reads the virtualizer's window.
- [Core: focus and virtualization](/docs/core/navigation) for `visibleRange`, the arithmetic under the virtualizer.
- [Row virtualization](/docs/react/row-virtualization) and [infinite scroll](/docs/react/infinite-scroll) for the React grid's props.

docs.title: Overlays
docs.description: attachOverlay places a panel beside an anchor, moves focus and stacks; placeOverlay is its arithmetic; the context menu trigger asks for one.
docs.body:
An overlay is a panel shown above the page beside an anchor: a menu, a popover, a filter editor. `attachOverlay` positions it, moves focus into it and reports when it should close; `placeOverlay` is its placement arithmetic on its own; and `attachContextMenuTrigger` reports the right-clicks, keys and long-presses that ask for a context menu, with the point to open one at. The menus drawn inside an overlay are on [menus and toolbar](/docs/dom/menus-and-toolbar), and the checklist a filter popup holds on [gestures and focus](/docs/dom/gestures-and-focus#checklist).

## Overlay

`attachOverlay(anchor, panel, options)` shows a panel the renderer has already put in the page — a menu, a popover, a filter editor, usually rendered into `document.body` so no scrolling ancestor clips it — beside `anchor`, an element or an `{ x, y }` point, and returns the function that ends it.

```ts
import { attachOverlay } from "@gridkitjs/dom";

const detach = attachOverlay(headerCell, menuElement, {
  placement: "bottom-start",
  gap: 4,
  onDismiss: (reason) => closeMenu(), // removes menuElement, then calls detach()
});
```

| Option                   | Type                                                        | Description                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `placement`              | `"bottom-start"`, `"top-end"`, `"right-start"` and the rest | Where the panel would rather open. Defaults to `"bottom-start"`.                                               |
| `gap`                    | `number`                                                    | Pixels between the anchor and the panel. Defaults to `0`.                                                      |
| `offset`                 | `number`                                                    | Pixels to shift the panel along the anchor's edge (below). Defaults to `0`.                                    |
| `onDismiss`              | `(reason) => void`                                          | Called with the reason the overlay asks to close (below); the caller closes the panel, or not.                 |
| `initialFocus`           | `"first"`, `"panel"`, `"none"` or an `HTMLElement`          | Where focus goes on attaching (below). Defaults to `"first"`.                                                  |
| `returnFocusTo`          | `HTMLElement \| null`                                       | Where focus goes on detach. Defaults to the element focused when the overlay attached; `null` leaves it alone. |
| `ignoreScrollAfterInput` | `boolean`                                                   | Whether a scroll just after input in the panel leaves it open (below). Defaults to `false`.                    |
| `trapFocus`              | `boolean`                                                   | Whether <Kbd>Tab</Kbd> cycles inside the panel ([below](#focus-trap)). Defaults to `false`.                    |

The panel is positioned `fixed` and opens on the preferred side unless only the opposite side has room for it, lines up with the preferred edge of the anchor unless only the other edge keeps it on screen, and is pushed back inside the viewport if it still overflows. The placement it ends up with is written to `data-gridkit-placement`. Whenever the panel's own size changes — a list that shrinks under a search, content that loads in — it is placed again from the anchor's current box and the same preferred placement, so a panel flipped above its anchor keeps its bottom edge against it. An anchor taken out of the page while the panel is open — the header of a column the panel just hid — leaves it placed beside where that anchor last was.

`offset` moves the panel along the edge it lines up with: down beside a `left` or `right` side, right beside `top` or `bottom`; a negative offset goes the other way. A submenu opened `right-start` passes its own top padding, negated, so its first item lines up with the item that opened it. The edge is chosen for the shifted panel, and it is still kept on screen.

Focus moves to the panel's first focusable element (`"first"`), or to the panel itself when it has none; `"panel"` focuses the panel itself, given `tabindex="-1"` when it has no `tabindex`; `"none"` leaves focus where it was, for a popup the user keeps typing past; an element focuses that element — a filter editor's value box rather than the operator picker before it, say.

It asks to close with one of these reasons. Nothing on the anchor counts, so a button that toggles the panel closes it with its own click.

| Reason      | When                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"escape"`  | <Kbd>Escape</Kbd> was pressed while it was the topmost overlay.                                                                                                                                                              |
| `"outside"` | A pointer went down outside it and outside every overlay above it.                                                                                                                                                           |
| `"scroll"`  | Something outside it scrolled — it is placed in viewport coordinates, so the anchor would move away from it. With `ignoreScrollAfterInput`, not in the two animation frames after an `input` or `change` event in the panel. |
| `"resize"`  | The window resized.                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `"blur"`    | The window lost focus, or focus moved somewhere outside it and outside every overlay above it.                                                                                                                               |
| `"parent"`  | The overlay it was opened above detached. It is detached straight after, whatever the caller does with the dismissal.                                                                                                        |

A panel whose controls change the page under it passes `ignoreScrollAfterInput`, so that what its own controls cause does not close it: a column chooser hiding a column narrows a grid scrolled to its end, and the browser scrolls that grid back within its narrower content. A scroll the user makes outside the panel still closes it.

Detaching returns focus only while focus is still in the panel, in an overlay above it, or nowhere — after a click on another control, focus stays there.

### Focus trap

A dialog-like panel — a filter editor with its own OK and Cancel — passes `trapFocus` so the keyboard cannot leave it by accident. <Kbd>Tab</Kbd> from its last tabbable element moves to its first, and <Kbd>Shift</Kbd>+<Kbd>Tab</Kbd> from its first to its last; every other <Kbd>Tab</Kbd> is the browser's own. Tabbable means focusable without a negative `tabindex`, enabled and shown, read afresh on each key so controls drawn since attaching count. A panel with nothing tabbable keeps focus where it is. Only the keys are kept in: a pointer down outside still dismisses it with `"outside"`, and focus moved outside by a script still dismisses it with `"blur"`. <Kbd>Tab</Kbd> in an overlay above it is that overlay's, and <Kbd>Escape</Kbd> and <Kbd>Enter</Kbd> are left alone — the stack still closes the topmost overlay on <Kbd>Escape</Kbd>, and the panel's own form hears <Kbd>Enter</Kbd>.

### Stacking

Overlays stack in the order they attach, so a submenu opened from a menu, or a picker opened from a filter panel, sits above the overlay it came from.

- <Kbd>Escape</Kbd> belongs to the topmost overlay alone: it is asked to close
  and the key goes no further — it is taken in the capture phase on `window`,
  before anything else on the page hears it. A grid that clears its selection on
  <Kbd>Escape</Kbd>, or a dialog that closes on it, is not disturbed by an
  <Kbd>Escape</Kbd> that closed a menu, and a second <Kbd>Escape</Kbd> closes
  the overlay below. With no overlay open, <Kbd>Escape</Kbd> passes through
  untouched.
- An overlay counts everything inside the overlays above it as inside itself: a click or a focus move into a submenu keeps its menu open, while a click elsewhere in the menu closes only the submenu, and a click outside both closes both.
- Detaching an overlay first dismisses every overlay still above it with `"parent"` and detaches it, topmost first, so a submenu never outlives its menu.

## Placement

`placeOverlay(anchorRect, panelSize, viewport, { placement, gap, offset })` is the placement on its own: pure arithmetic over boxes, returning `{ top, left, placement }`, for a renderer that positions its own panels.

## Context menu trigger

`attachContextMenuTrigger(root, { onRequest })` reports every context menu the user asks for inside `root` — a right-click, <Kbd>Shift</Kbd>+<Kbd>F10</Kbd>, the <Kbd>ContextMenu</Kbd> key, or a touch held still for half a second — and returns the function that stops it. `onRequest` is called with a `ContextMenuRequest` and answers whether it opened a menu of its own: `true` prevents the browser's menu, `false` lets it show, so a part of the grid with nothing to offer keeps the browser's.

| Field    | Type                      | Description                                                                                                                  |
| -------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `target` | `Element`                 | The element under the pointer, or the focused one for a key.                                                                 |
| `point`  | `{ x, y } \| null`        | Where the pointer was, in viewport coordinates — an overlay anchor as it is. `null` from the keyboard: open beside `target`. |
| `source` | `"pointer" \| "keyboard"` | How it was asked for: a right-click or a long-press, or a key.                                                               |

```ts
import { attachContextMenuTrigger, attachOverlay } from "@gridkitjs/dom";

const stop = attachContextMenuTrigger(gridElement, {
  onRequest: ({ target, point }) => {
    const cell = target.closest("td[data-gridkit-column]");
    if (cell === null) return false; // the browser's menu, then
    showMenu(point ?? cell); // an attachOverlay anchor: the point, or the cell
    return true;
  },
});
```

Each gesture asks once. On some systems a key press also makes the browser fire a `contextmenu` event of its own; once the key opened a menu, that event is taken rather than reported again.

A long-press is a primary touch that rests for 500 ms, drifting no more than 10 pixels; one that moves further, lifts sooner or is taken over by the browser to scroll asks nothing, and a mouse or pen held down never asks. It is reported with the touch's point. A browser that turns a held touch into a `contextmenu` of its own — Chrome on Android does — asks once, whichever comes first. Once a long-press opened a menu, the click its lifting brings is taken before anything under the finger hears it: the menu opened there, and a click would land in it.

An event something already prevented is left alone, so a cell template with a menu of its own keeps it. For that, the trigger listens on the document in the bubble phase — after a framework that handles events at its root container, as React does, where a listener on `root` would hear them first — and counts only events whose target is inside `root`.

## Types

| Type                        | Description                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `OverlayOptions`            | The last argument of `attachOverlay`: the `OverlayPlacementOptions` plus `onDismiss`, `initialFocus`, `returnFocusTo`, `ignoreScrollAfterInput` and `trapFocus`, as tabled under [overlay](#overlay). |
| `OverlayAnchor`             | What an overlay opens beside: an `Element`, or a `{ x, y }` point in viewport coordinates.                                                                                                            |
| `OverlayInitialFocus`       | `"first"`, `"panel"`, `"none"` or an `HTMLElement`: where focus goes on attaching.                                                                                                                    |
| `OverlayDismissReason`      | `"escape"`, `"outside"`, `"scroll"`, `"resize"`, `"blur"` or `"parent"`, each tabled under [overlay](#overlay).                                                                                       |
| `OverlayPlacementOptions`   | `{ placement?, gap?, offset? }`, shared by `attachOverlay` and `placeOverlay`.                                                                                                                        |
| `OverlayPlacement`          | A side and an alignment joined by a dash: `"bottom-start"`, `"top-end"`, `"right-start"` and the other five.                                                                                          |
| `OverlaySide`               | `"top"`, `"bottom"`, `"left"` or `"right"`.                                                                                                                                                           |
| `OverlayAlign`              | `"start"` or `"end"`: which edge of the anchor the panel lines up with.                                                                                                                               |
| `OverlayRect`               | `{ top, left, width, height }`: the anchor's box for `placeOverlay`, in viewport coordinates. A point is a box with no width or height.                                                               |
| `OverlaySize`               | `{ width, height }`: the panel's size, and the viewport's.                                                                                                                                            |
| `OverlayPosition`           | `{ top, left, placement }`, what `placeOverlay` returns, with the placement the panel ended up with.                                                                                                  |
| `ContextMenuTriggerOptions` | `{ onRequest }`, the last argument of `attachContextMenuTrigger`.                                                                                                                                     |
| `ContextMenuRequest`        | `{ target, point, source }`, tabled under [context menu trigger](#context-menu-trigger).                                                                                                              |
| `ContextMenuSource`         | `"pointer"` for a right-click or a long-press, `"keyboard"` for a key.                                                                                                                                |

## See also

- [Menus and toolbar](/docs/dom/menus-and-toolbar) for the menus shown in an overlay.
- [Overview](/docs/dom) for the contract every behaviour follows.
- [Core: commands and menus](/docs/core/commands#menus) for what a context menu lists.
- [Context menu](/docs/react/context-menu) for the menus the React grid opens with these.

docs.title: Overview
docs.description: Framework-free browser behaviours for GridKit renderers: gestures, focus, observers, virtualization, overlays, menus, toolbars, downloads, clipboard.
docs.body:
@gridkitjs/dom holds every browser behaviour a grid needs that is not drawing: pointer gestures, keyboard focus movement, the observers behind fit-to-width and infinite scroll, the row virtualizer's measuring, overlays and the menus and checklists shown in them, toolbars, the live region it reports changes through, the download an export ends in, the clipboard a copy goes to, and the hidden frame a print goes through. @gridkitjs/core decides what the grid does and runs without a DOM; @gridkitjs/dom does what needs one, with no framework; a renderer such as @gridkitjs/react draws the markup and attaches these behaviours to it. A second renderer — for Angular, Vue or Svelte — reuses both unchanged.

You only need this package to write a renderer of your own. @gridkitjs/react depends on it already, so installing that is enough to use the grid.

## Install

<PackageInstall pkg="@gridkitjs/dom" />

## The contract

Every behaviour is attached to elements the renderer already drew and handed options, owns its own listeners and observers, reports through callbacks, and gives back the way to end it — a function, or an object with `detach` or `destroy`. None names a framework's types, so each maps onto a framework's own lifecycle: a React ref callback or effect, an Angular directive and `ngOnDestroy`, a Vue `onMounted`, a Svelte action.

```ts
const detach = observeElementWidth(element, (width) => {
  /* … */
});
// later, when the element goes away:
detach();
```

Where a behaviour reads the grid's markup, it relies on the attributes @gridkitjs/react renders — `data-gridkit-column` on header and body cells, `data-gridkit-row-index` on body rows, `data-gridkit-group-by-bar` and `data-gridkit-group-chip` on the group-by bar — so a renderer that draws the same markup gets the same behaviour. What a behaviour reports that changes how the grid looks — a drop target, the window of rows, the focused cell — is the renderer's to draw; what changes the grid's state goes through the controller's actions.

## Pages

  <LinkCard
    href="/docs/dom/gestures-and-focus"
    title="Gestures and focus"
    description="Body event targets, column resize and reorder drags, grid and checklist focus, and the live announcer."
  />
  <LinkCard

    title="Overlays"
    description="Placing a panel beside an anchor, focus, dismissal, stacking and the context menu trigger."
  />
  <LinkCard

    title="Menus and toolbar"
    description="The menu and toolbar keyboard patterns, submenus, and toolbar overflow."
  />
  <LinkCard
    href="/docs/dom/observers-and-virtualizer"
    title="Observers and virtualizer"
    description="Element width, the row virtualizer and infinite scroll."
  />
  <LinkCard
    href="/docs/dom/downloads-clipboard-print"
    title="Downloads, clipboard and print"
    description="Saving an export, writing the clipboard and printing through a hidden frame."
  />
</LinkCards>

## Exports by page

Every export of `@gridkitjs/dom`, and the page that documents it:

| Page                                                                  | Functions and values                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Types                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [Gestures and focus](/docs/dom/gestures-and-focus)                    | `bodyCellFrom`, `groupRowFrom`, `bodyRowFrom`, `startColumnResizeGesture`, `measureColumnContent`, `startDragReorder`, `NO_DRAG`, `resolveColumnDropTarget`, `resolveGroupByDropTarget`, `createGridFocus`, `findBodyRow`, `measurePageSize`, `attachChecklist`, `createLiveAnnouncer` | `BodyCellTarget`, `GroupRowTarget`, `BodyRowTarget`, `PointerPress`, `ColumnResizeGestureHandlers`, `DragReorderState`, `DragReorderHandlers`, `ColumnDropTarget`, `GroupByDropTarget`, `ColumnDropContext`, `GridFocusOptions`, `GridFocusController`, `GridFocusRows`, `FocusVirtualRange`, `ChecklistOptions`, `AttachedChecklist`, `LiveAnnouncer` |
| [Overlays](/docs/dom/overlays)                                        | `attachOverlay`, `placeOverlay`, `attachContextMenuTrigger`                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | `OverlayOptions`, `OverlayAnchor`, `OverlayInitialFocus`, `OverlayDismissReason`, `OverlayPlacementOptions`, `OverlayPlacement`, `OverlaySide`, `OverlayAlign`, `OverlayRect`, `OverlaySize`, `OverlayPosition`, `ContextMenuTriggerOptions`, `ContextMenuRequest`, `ContextMenuSource`                                                                |
| [Menus and toolbar](/docs/dom/menus-and-toolbar)                      | `attachMenu`, `attachToolbar`, `observeToolbarOverflow`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | `MenuOptions`, `AttachedMenu`, `MenuSubmenuFocus`, `MenuCloseReason`, `ToolbarOverflowOptions`, `ToolbarOverflowItem`, `ToolbarOverflow`                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| [Observers and virtualizer](/docs/dom/observers-and-virtualizer)      | `observeElementWidth`, `createRowVirtualizer`, `attachInfiniteScroll`                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | `RowVirtualizerOptions`, `RowVirtualizer`, `InfiniteScrollOptions`, `InfiniteScroll`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

docs.title: Overview
docs.description: Export a GridKit grid to Excel: numbers and dates stored typed, a frozen header, column widths, group outlines and the grand total.
docs.body:
@gridkitjs/export-xlsx turns what a grid shows into an Excel workbook. It is an [export writer](/docs/core/export#writers): you register it on the grid, and the grid's "Export to Excel" command appears — in the toolbar's [Export dropdown](/docs/react/export#from-the-toolbar), in the context menu where export commands are listed, and behind `ref.current.exportData("xlsx")`. The workbook is built from the same table as every other export, so it holds the rows, columns, groups and totals a CSV would, with the cells typed.

It is a package of its own so that the grid stays free of dependencies for those who never export to Excel. It depends on @gridkitjs/core and [fflate](https://www.npmjs.com/package/fflate), a small zip library, and on no DOM: it runs in the browser, in Node, and under any renderer.

## Install

<PackageInstall pkg="@gridkitjs/export-xlsx" />

## Register it

<ExportExample />

```tsx
import { DataGrid } from "@gridkitjs/react";
import { xlsxWriter } from "@gridkitjs/export-xlsx";

const writers = [xlsxWriter({ sheetName: "Orders" })];

<DataGrid
  columns={columns}
  dataSource={orders}
  toolbar={{ items: ["export"] }}
  exportWriters={writers}
/>;
```

Make the writer once, outside the component or in a `useMemo`, as you would any other prop that should not change on every render. Choosing "Export to Excel" downloads `export.xlsx` — the grid's [`export.fileName`](/docs/react/export#options) names it — and "Export selection to Excel" appears beside it while rows are selected.

To get the file without downloading it, ask the ref:

```ts
const blob = await gridRef.current?.exportData("xlsx");
```

## Options

`xlsxWriter(options)` takes an `XlsxWriterOptions` object, exported as a type from the package. Every field is optional:

| Option       | Type                                                  | Default    | Description                                                                                                                              |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sheetName`  | `string`                                              | `"Sheet1"` | The sheet's name. Excel allows 31 characters and none of `[ ] : * ? / \`, so a longer name is cut and those characters become `_`.       |
| `headerRows` | `readonly string[] \| (context) => readonly string[]` | none       | Lines of text above the header row, each a row of its own in the first column. A function is asked per export with the writer's context. |
| `values`     | `"typed" \| "text"`                                   | `"typed"`  | `"typed"` stores numbers, dates and booleans as Excel's own; `"text"` writes every cell as the text the grid shows, as CSV does.         |

`headerRows` is where a report's title goes, with when it was exported and what it was run with. Given as a function, it is asked at each export, so the date is that export's:

```ts
xlsxWriter({
  headerRows: ({ locale }) => [
    "Orders by region",
    `Exported ${new Date().toLocaleString(locale)}`,
    "",
  ],
});
```

An empty string leaves a blank row. The title rows are frozen with the header row, so they stay in view as the sheet scrolls.

## What goes where

| In the grid                             | In the workbook                                                                                                   |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The header row                          | The first row (after any `headerRows`), bold, frozen, and repeated at the top of every printed page.              |
| A column's width                        | The column's width, at about 7px to Excel's character.                                                            |
| A number                                | A number, in a format read from the column — see below.                                                           |
| A `Date`                                | A date: the local calendar date and time the grid shows, in a date format — see below.                            |
| A boolean                               | `TRUE` or `FALSE`.                                                                                                |
| Text                                    | Text, as the grid shows it — a `valueFormatter`'s text rather than the raw value.                                 |
